blocks.content: Volume-related problems tend to look confusing because the symptom (a permission error, missing data) often shows up far from the actual cause (a UID mismatch, the wrong kind of mount).
1. "Permission Denied" Writing to a Mounted Volume
blocks.text: 1. "Permission Denied" Writing to a Mounted Volume

blocks.content: This is usually a UID mismatch: the container process (running as a specific UID, per the USER instruction covered in the Docker Security module) does not have permission to write to files owned by a different UID on the host side of a bind mount, or in an existing volume.

blocks.alt: The container's UID doesn't have permission to write there

blocks.content:
docker exec web id
# Confirm exactly which UID the container is running as,
# then compare against the ownership of the mounted path.

code.content:
docker exec web id
# Confirm exactly which UID the container is running as,
# then compare against the ownership of the mounted path.

codes.bash:
docker exec web id
# Confirm exactly which UID the container is running as,
# then compare against the ownership of the mounted path.

blocks.content: 2. "My Data Disappeared After Recreating the Container"
blocks.text: 2. "My Data Disappeared After Recreating the Container"

blocks.content: This almost always traces back to the Anonymous Volumes topic: if the path was never actually mounted as a named volume, or a bind mount, in the first place, its data lived only in the old container's writable layer or an anonymous volume that got cleaned up, not somewhere that would survive recreation at all.

blocks.alt: Was there actually a named volume or bind mount there at all?

blocks.content: 3. A Bind Mount Silently Mounting an Empty Directory
blocks.text: 3. A Bind Mount Silently Mounting an Empty Directory

blocks.content: A typo in a bind mount's host path does not error out, Docker simply creates a new, empty directory at that (wrong) path and mounts it, the container starts fine, but the expected files are simply not there, a genuinely easy mistake to make and a confusing one to spot.

blocks.alt: A typo creates an empty directory instead of failing loudly

blocks.content: Rather than guessing, docker inspect (for the container's Mounts section) or docker volume inspect (for a named volume specifically) shows exactly what is mounted where, including the real host path behind a bind mount.

blocks.alt: Confirm the actual mount configuration directly

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A permission error on a mounted path is usually a UID mismatch between the container's user and the file's ownership.
Missing data after a recreate, or a mount that seems empty, almost always traces back to the wrong mount type (anonymous instead of named) or a silent path typo.
